analysis_steps.goal: Extrapolate 3D coronal and chromospheric magnetic field from photospheric magnetogram

method.value: Perform linear force-free field (LFF) extrapolation above the photosphere starting from the line-of-sight magnetic field component to generate 3D cubes of Bx, By, Bz and field line positions, and interpolate voxel height resolution to 50 km.

evidence.quote: Photospheric magnetograms are used as the boundary condition for an extrapolation of the field above the photosphere using the linear force-free field approximation.
The result is three cubes of intensities, one for each component of the magnetic field vector ($B_x$, $B_y$, and $B_z$) and another data cube for the positions of the magnetic field lines.

However, the radiative transfer calculations require better resolution in the height of the voxels ($h_z$) due to the relatively narrow width of the chromosphere, and they were re-scaled via interpolation from the resolution of the magnetogram to 50 km, similar to the resolution of the SSC model.

A low value for the $\alpha$ parameter in (1) does not significantly affect the extrapolated magnetic field configuration at low heights in the atmosphere: here $\alpha=-0.005$ was chosen for the LFF extrapolation since it generated a greater number of closed magnetic field lines in the selected region than did the potential-field extrapolation ($\alpha=0$).
In this work, the extrapolated field lines were calculated only above positions with $|\vec{B}|_{min}=200$ G at the photosphere.

analysis_steps.goal: Classify pixels by photospheric magnetic field strength

method.value: Classify each pixel in the magnetogram into four classes based on photospheric magnetic field intensity |B|_0: umbra, penumbra, plage, and quiet Sun.

evidence.quote: The resulting atmospheric profiles were grouped into four different classes corresponding to different atmospheric features: umbrae, penumbrae, plage and quiet Sun.

Each pixel in the magnetogram was classified as umbra, penumbra, or plage according to its intensity ($|\vec{B}|$), as follows: umbra, $|\vec{B}|\geq1500$ G ($\sim200$ pixels); penumbra, $1000\leq |\vec{B}_0|<1500$ G ($\sim$230 pixels); plages, $200\leq|\vec{B}_0|<1000$ G ($\sim$27200 pixels). All pixels with $|\vec{B}|\leq200$ G were classified as quiet Sun ($\sim$38000 pixels) and were assumed to have $T_B=T_{qS}$.

analysis_steps.goal: Fit 1D atmospheric temperature and density profiles per pixel via genetic algorithm and radiative transfer

method.value: Run Pikaia genetic algorithm independently for each vertical column (pixel) to modify the seed SSC quiet Sun model via 5 free parameters, compute thermal bremsstrahlung and gyroresonance absorption coefficients and 1D radiative transfer to obtain T_b at 17, 100, and 230 GHz, minimize chi-squared against observations, and average best-fit profiles per class.

evidence.quote: An initial 1D atmospheric model is used as a seed for the GA: at each step, $T_\mathrm{b}$ is obtained via the calculation of radiative transfer incorporating opacity from both the thermal bremsstrahlung and gyroresonance emission mechanisms.
The GA iteratively updates the atmospheric plasma trapped by magnetic field lines until a best model is found via $\chi^2$ minimization of the calculated and observed $T_\mathrm{b}$ values.

We then obtained the average electron density and temperature profiles for each of the three AR classes by calculating the average of the profiles with the lowest $\chi^2$ values in the $T_\mathrm{b}$ calculation, in relation to the observed values at the three distinct observing frequencies.

key_parameters.value: 5 free parameters: chromospheric temperature gradient, chromospheric electron density gradient, coronal temperature factor N_T, coronal electron density factor N_n_e, and TR position shift Delta h

evidence.quote: Five free parameters are supplied to the GA representing the atmospheric model.

key_parameters.value: GA settings: full-generation replacement, 10 generations, 100 children per generation, crossover probability = 0.85, variable mutation mode, initial mutation rate = 0.005, mutation rate range = 0.0005 to 0.25

evidence.quote: The method used here was full-generation replacement using ten generations with one hundred children each. The crossover probability was 0.85 and the mutation mode was variable. The initial mutation rate, that is, the initial probability that any gene locus will mutate in any generation, was 0.005. Finally, the mutation rate range was between 0.0005 and 0.25.

key_parameters.value: Gyroresonance harmonics s <= 5 with 10% uncertainty in |B| (3rd harmonic at 2000±200 G, 4th at 1500±150 G, 5th at 1200±120 G)

evidence.quote: Since the contribution of higher harmonics to the radio emission is very small (cite: Shibasaki1994), the gyroresonance emission was only calculated for harmonics smaller than 5 ($s\leq 5$).
To investigate the gyroresonance contribution, $\kappa_g$ was calculated for harmonics $s\leq 5$, allowing for an uncertainty of $10\%$ in the $|\vec{B}|$ values.

assumptions.value: Effective ion charge Z = 1.178, only electron-proton collisions considered, densities grouped as (n_e * n_i)^(1/2), plasma fully ionized above 1000 km in SSC model

evidence.quote: Only the contributions of collisions with protons was considered, since its density is much larger than that of other ion species ($n_i$).

Following (cite: Zirin1988), it was assumed $Z=1.178$, if a fully hydrogen atmosphere was considered, i.e. $Z=1$, the resulting $T_\mathrm{b}$ should be only $\sim 3\%$ smaller for all frequencies simulated here.
Although, the SSC model considers the plasma fully ionized above 1000 km, i.e. $n_e=n_i$, to simplify the GA the densities were grouped in a single variable, that is $(n_e\times n_i)^{1/2}$.

fitting.value: Pikaia genetic algorithm with chi-squared minimization; full-generation replacement over 10 generations with 100 children each; stabilizes by ~7th generation.

evidence.quote: A generation of child atmospheric models is created by the algorithm based on the parent models with the lowest $\chi^2$ values, using the genetic algorithm described in (cite: Charbonneau1995).
In our runs the $\chi^2$ measure typically stabilizes to a minimum value by about the seventh generation.

validation.value: Monitored stabilization of chi-squared across generations and evaluated optical depth and contribution functions across atmospheric layers.

evidence.quote: In our runs the $\chi^2$ measure typically stabilizes to a minimum value by about the seventh generation.

In Figure [5](#fig:tau_cf) we show, for each atmospheric class, the optical depth ($\tau$, top row) and the contribution function (CF, bottom row), that represents the emission variation with the atmosphere height.

findings_qualitative.value: Umbrae, penumbrae, and plages have a narrower temperature-minimum region and a thinner chromosphere than the quiet Sun, with compression most pronounced in umbral pixels.

evidence.quote: Comparison with the quiet-Sun model indicates that the umbrae, penumbrae and plages have a narrower temperature-minimum region and a thinner chromosphere than the quiet Sun, as can be seen in Table [\[Table:profile\]](#Table:profile) and Figure [4](#fig:temp_dens).
Moreover, the compression of the temperature minimum and the chromosphere are most pronounced in umbral pixels, i.e. the region with more intense magnetic fields (Figure [4](#fig:temp_dens)).

findings_qualitative.value: The umbral region is the only region presenting a significant increase in coronal temperature, required to produce the high 17 GHz gyroresonance brightness temperatures.

evidence.quote: Furthermore, the umbral region is the only one that presents a significant increase in the coronal temperature, which is necessary to reach the high $T_\mathrm{b}$ values observed in the gyroresonance source at 17 GHz (cite: Selhorst2008; Selhorst2009).

findings_qualitative.value: At 17 GHz in the umbral core, the 3rd gyroresonance harmonic occurs between 1150 and 1900 km and provides an optical depth tau ~ 0.1 (three orders of magnitude larger than free-free), producing a contribution function peak ~20 times larger than free-free.

evidence.quote: The 3rd harmonic occurs between 1150 and 1900 km in altitude, while the 4th harmonic occurs between 2550 and 4050 km.

The 3rd harmonic provides an optical depth of $\tau\sim10^{-1}$ (Figure [6](#fig:kappa17)b red curve) that is three orders of magnitude greater than the free-free optical depth (Figure [6](#fig:kappa17)b black curve).

While the free-free CF shows a single peak at around 800 km (black curve), when the gyroresonance is included an intense peak appears at TR/coronal heights (red curve) that is $\sim 20$ times greater than the free-free contribution.

claims.hypothesis: A genetic algorithm modifying a 1D quiet Sun atmospheric model along 3D linear force-free extrapolated magnetic field lines can determine temperature and electron density profiles that reproduce observed active region brightness temperatures at 17, 100, and 230 GHz.
claims.experiment: Applied the Pikaia genetic algorithm with 5 free parameters per pixel to AR NOAA 12470 using SDO/HMI magnetograms, ALMA 100 and 230 GHz single-dish maps, and NoRH 17 GHz maps, computing thermal bremsstrahlung and gyroresonance radiative transfer.
claims.result: Derived distinct transition region heights for umbrae (1080 ± 20 km), penumbrae (1800 ± 50 km), and plages (2000 ± 100 km); simulated 230 and 100 GHz brightness temperatures match observations within uncertainties across all AR regions, and 17 GHz polarized emission matches when gyroresonance is included (4.08 ± 1.19 vs 3.69 ± 1.35 T_qS).
claims.finding: The GA-constrained atmospheric model successfully reproduces the ALMA 100 and 230 GHz maps and the 17 GHz polarized gyroresonance core, though it underpredicts the maximum T_b in 17 GHz non-polarized regions (1.2 vs 2.8 T_qS).

evidence.quote: for umbrae the TR is located at $1080\pm20$ km above the solar surface; for penumbrae, the TR is located at $1800\pm50$ km; and for bright regions outside sunspots, the TR is located at $2000\pm100$ km. With these results, we find good agreement with the observed AR brightness temperature maps.

claims.hypothesis: The dark sunspot umbra observed at 230 GHz and the bright polarized core at 17 GHz arise from a compressed chromosphere/transition region in strong magnetic fields combined with 17 GHz gyroresonance opacity in the corona/TR.
claims.experiment: Evaluated optical depths and contribution functions for free-free and gyroresonance (s <= 5) emission in the umbral atmospheric model and compared synthetic images with and without gyroresonance and beam convolution.
claims.result: At 230 GHz the unconvolved model umbra is darker than the quiet Sun (0.98 ± 0.01 T_qS, smoothed to 1.00 ± 0.01 T_qS at 25" resolution); at 17 GHz, free-free alone yields a dark umbra (1.06 ± 0.02 T_qS), whereas including 3rd and 4th harmonic gyroresonance opacity (tau ~ 0.1) increases T_b to 4.08 ± 1.19 T_qS at 10" resolution.
claims.finding: Thermal free-free emission from a compressed umbral atmosphere produces a dark umbra at millimeter wavelengths (and would at 17 GHz if alone), while 3rd-harmonic gyroresonance opacity in the hot umbral corona/TR dominates at 17 GHz to produce the bright polarized core.

evidence.loc: Comparison of the synthetic and observed radio images
evidence.quote: Even though dark when compared with the surrounding areas, the umbral $T_\mathrm{b}$ is only smaller than the $T_\mathrm{b,QS}$ in the 230 GHz observation, and in the model result without the beam convolution, as shown in Table [\[Table:mean\]](#Table:mean).

evidence.loc: Comparison of the synthetic and observed radio images
evidence.quote: If only free-free emission is considered, at 17 GHz the umbra appears darker in the model than the surrounding area, with a brightness temperature of $1.06\pm0.02\times T_{qS}$ at 10” resolution. When gyroresonance is included, the modeled $T_\mathrm{b}$ increased to values above $10 \times T_{qS}$.

Moreover, if only thermal free-free emission was contributing opacity at 17 GHz, the AR umbra should look darker than the surrounding region (see Figure [7](#fig:NoRH)b) and probably darker than the quiet Sun as the high resolution ALMA interferometric data suggest.

why_this_data.value: AR NOAA 12470 was selected due to the availability of multi-frequency radio observations at 17 GHz (NoRH) and 100 and 230 GHz (ALMA Science Verification) along with SDO/HMI magnetograms, probing distinct atmospheric layers.

evidence.quote: The different frequencies provide access to different layers of the atmosphere due to the frequency dependence of opacity.

In this work, we selected the active region AR NOAA 12470 to test our algorithm. This region was selected due to the availability of radio observations at three frequencies: 17 GHz, from the Nobeyama Radio Heliograph (NoRH), 100 and 230 GHz from the Atacama Large Millimetric and submillimetric Array (ALMA) (cite: Shimojo2017; Valle2021).

why_this_method.value: A genetic algorithm modifying a seed quiet Sun model along 3D LFF extrapolated magnetic fields improves upon manual semi-empirical modeling (Selhorst et al. 2008, 2009) and PFSS modeling (Brajša et al. 2020) by automatically optimizing temperature and density profiles per pixel.

evidence.quote: As an improvement of the AR modelling presented in (cite: Selhorst2008; Selhorst2009), in this work we apply a genetic algorithm (cite: Charbonneau1995) to modify a standard quiet Sun atmospheric model in order to determine the best plasma temperature and density height profiles necessary to match the observations of NOAA 12470 obtained by ALMA (single-dish maps at 100 and 230 GHz) and NoRH (17 GHz interferometric map).

The general extrapolated magnetic structure is consistent with the ALMA observations, but a detailed analysis and comparison with ALMA small-scale features was not possible with the model used and requires a more detailed magnetic field extrapolation model, what is performed in the present work.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Potential-field extrapolation (alpha = 0) was rejected in favor of alpha = -0.005 because alpha = -0.005 generated a greater number of closed magnetic field lines in the selected region.

evidence.quote: here $\alpha=-0.005$ was chosen for the LFF extrapolation since it generated a greater number of closed magnetic field lines in the selected region than did the potential-field extrapolation ($\alpha=0$).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Including photospheric magnetic fields below |B|_min = 200 G was rejected because it resulted in simulated ARs appearing much larger than observed ARs.

evidence.quote: A different minimum value could be chosen by the user, but we found that the inclusion of magnetic fields below this limit resulted in the simulated ARs appearing much larger than the observed ARs.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Classifying AR regions using white light images (as in Nita et al. 2018) was rejected in favor of magnetogram field intensity thresholds because white light separation is not useful for faint or spotless ARs.

evidence.quote: In (cite: Nita2018), the authors proposed a similar separation, however, in that work the separation was based on solar white light images instead of a magnetogram, which is not useful for faint or spotless ARs.

how_they_decided_enough.value: The GA was run for 10 generations of 100 children because chi-squared typically stabilizes by about the 7th generation, stopping when chi-squared ceases to reduce further.

evidence.quote: In our runs the $\chi^2$ measure typically stabilizes to a minimum value by about the seventh generation.
The final model is obtained when the $\chi^2$ from the GA process ceases to reduce further.

limitations_admitted.value: The genetic algorithm is purely a mathematical solution and does not verify whether the atmospheric plasma is in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE).

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, the GA used here is a mathematical solution and it does not verify if the atmospheric plasma is in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) or not.

limitations_admitted.value: Low spatial resolution of ALMA single-dish observations (25" at 230 GHz, 58" at 100 GHz) smooths the dark umbra (25" diameter) with surrounding bright areas, masking the umbra at 100 GHz and reducing its contrast at 230 GHz.

evidence.loc: Comparison of the synthetic and observed radio images
evidence.quote: The resulting low contrast of the dark umbra with respect to the quiet Sun in the model is due to the low resolution of the ALMA single-dish observations. Since the umbral size is almost equal to the ALMA 230 GHz beam, the umbral $T_\mathrm{b}$ is smoothed with the bright surrounding areas.

limitations_admitted.value: The modeled atmospheric profiles that fit 230 and 100 GHz well cannot reach the high brightness temperatures observed at 17 GHz in non-polarized regions (reaching at most 1.2 T_qS vs. 2.8 T_qS observed).

evidence.loc: Comparison of the synthetic and observed radio images
evidence.quote: However, the modeled atmospheric profiles that achieved good agreement with the $T_\mathrm{b}$ observations at 230 and 100 GHz were not able to reach the high $T_\mathrm{b}$ values observed at 17 GHz. While these regions showed observational values as high as $2.8\times T_{qS}$, the model was only able to reach a maximum $T_\mathrm{b}$ of $1.2\times T_{qS}$ (Figure [7](#fig:NoRH)b).

limitations_admitted.value: The modeled 17 GHz polarized gyroresonance source is smaller and rounder than the observed elliptical source.

evidence.loc: Comparison of the synthetic and observed radio images
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, as can be observed in Figure [\[emiss_giro3\]](#emiss_giro3), the shape of the modelled polarized region is smaller and rounder, while the observed source appears elliptical.

referee_caveats_inferred: Fitting 5 free parameters per pixel against only 3 frequency data points (17, 100, and 230 GHz) is an under-constrained optimization problem per line of sight, relying heavily on parameter bounds and initial class seeds that are not explicitly tabulated.

The pixel-by-pixel GA optimization compares 2" model columns against observed maps that have vastly different beam sizes (58" at 100 GHz, 25" at 230 GHz, 10-18" at 17 GHz) before final beam convolution, introducing beam-dilution biases into the un-deconvolved pixel fits.

The observations at the three frequencies are non-simultaneous (02:44 UT at 17 GHz, 14:52 UT at 230 GHz, 19:35 UT at 100 GHz), spanning nearly 17 hours during which solar active region evolution can occur.
